title: Stable Falsehoods in Large Language Models: A Consistency-Based Approach to Hallucination Analysis Creators Niall Devlin (Concept Originator) Affiliation (if desired): Rotherham Metropolitan Borough Council Service Director, Education & Inclusion Publication Date Use the date you submit/publish on Zenodo. Resource Type Publication → Preprint (recommended) Alternatively: Report (if you consider it a working paper) Software (for the prototype separately) Description / Abstract Most Large Language Model (LLM) evaluation frameworks focus primarily on factual correctness. This paper proposes an alternative perspective by examining the interaction between correctness and consistency. It introduces the concept of the Stable Falsehood: a response pattern in which a model repeatedly generates the same incorrect answer across multiple independent samples. The framework evaluates LLM behaviour using repeated fresh-context sampling and measures agreement, accuracy, entropy, and semantic similarity as separate dimensions. By analysing the relationship between correctness and consistency, the methodology classifies responses into behavioural categories including Stable Correct, Stable Falsehood, Variable Correct, Variable False, and Chaotic. The accompanying prototype, the Confabulation Variance Test (Research Edition v4), demonstrates practical implementation of the methodology through repeated sampling, statistical analysis, entropy measurement, and behavioural classification. The principal contribution is the systematic treatment of consistency and correctness as independent dimensions whose interaction reveals distinct forms of model reliability. The work argues that a model which is consistently wrong may represent a different and potentially more significant reliability challenge than a model which is inconsistently wrong.
